name: Revise
tagline: Always knows the next highest-value thing to revise.
summary: A revision-first study platform for UK A-level and GCSE. Every screen exists to raise a grade: open it, get one recommended task, complete it, get marked, watch progress move.

authorship.role: Sole author — product, curriculum data model and implementation.
built: The recommendation scorer that ranks due reviews, mistake repair, weak-topic practice, first-pass learning and timed papers on one scale
The board-agnostic curriculum module format, and the validator that enforces per-statement provenance on every spec point
Point-by-point marking against mark schemes, with mistakes automatically becoming flashcards
The adaptive timetable that rolls missed blocks forward
notBuilt: FSRS — the spaced-repetition scheduling algorithm is an existing published algorithm, not my work
Supabase (optional sync backend) and the model provider used for prose

caseStudy.problem: Revision tools are built as note-taking apps, so they optimise for capture. That leaves the one question that actually matters the week before an exam — what should I do right now? — entirely to the student, at exactly the moment they are least able to answer it.
caseStudy.approach: Score every candidate activity on a single scale and show the winner with a plain-English reason. Because everything competes on one number, a due flashcard, an unrepaired mistake and an untouched weak topic can be compared directly instead of living in separate tabs. The curriculum is data, not code: adding a board means adding one module and changing nothing else.

architecture.summary: Curriculum is data with provenance; scheduling, marking and planning are pure functions over it; storage is local-first with sync as an opt-in.
architecture.invariant: Every examinable statement carries its own verification metadata, so coverage figures describe checked content rather than merely present content.

layers.name: Curriculum modules
layers.role: One module per board/qualification. Topics, spec points and seed questions, each with source and verification stamps.

layers.name: Scheduling
layers.role: FSRS intervals, confidence captured before reveal, failed cards reinserted within the session.

layers.name: Marking
layers.role: Point-by-point comparison against the mark scheme; every dropped mark becomes a classified mistake and a flashcard.

layers.name: Planning
layers.role: Adaptive timetable derived from exam dates, availability, mastery and outstanding mistakes.

layers.name: Storage
layers.role: IndexedDB single local profile by default. Supabase sync and model-written prose are both optional.

visuals.alt: Illustration of a revision dashboard showing a streak counter, cards due today and a revision plan progress bar
visuals.caption: Illustration of the daily view. Not a screenshot — no capture of the running app has been published yet.

metrics.label: Automated tests
metrics.method: `npm test` in apps/revise. Count as stated in the project README; the portfolio's CI importer replaces this with the live figure from the Revise workflow when a run is readable.

metrics.label: Authored curriculum
metrics.method: Content counted by the repo's own curriculum validator, which also enforces per-subject statement-density floors.

outcomes.statement: Adding a new exam board requires one new curriculum module and no changes elsewhere — the board-agnostic split is real, not aspirational.
The app is fully usable with no environment variables at all: cards, marking, planning, analytics and search all work against a local profile.

tradeoffs.choice: Local-first IndexedDB as the default, sync as an opt-in
tradeoffs.gained: The app works with zero setup and no account, and a student's data never leaves their machine unless they ask for it.
tradeoffs.gaveUp: Cross-device revision is not available out of the box, which is a real cost for someone revising on both a laptop and a phone.

tradeoffs.choice: Curriculum as validated data modules rather than hardcoded content
tradeoffs.gained: New boards and qualifications are additive, and a validator can enforce provenance and density floors across all of them.
tradeoffs.gaveUp: Considerably more up-front work than hardcoding one syllabus, and every content change now has to satisfy the validator.

failedApproaches.approach: Topic-level provenance on curriculum content, with statement-level coverage computed on top of it.
failedApproaches.whyItFailed: Coverage was reported per statement but provenance was only recorded per topic, so the claim that every examinable statement was individually mapped was not actually true of the data.
failedApproaches.whatItChanged: Every spec point across all four science and maths curriculum files was migrated to carry its own verification, source, reviewer, last-checked date and spec version, so the reported coverage now reflects verification rather than mere presence.

lessons: A coverage number is only as honest as the granularity of the metadata underneath it. Reporting statement-level coverage from topic-level provenance quietly overstated what had been checked.
limitations: No external examiner blind study — marking agreement is measured against an internal double-marked corpus only.
Short-answer formats only; maths/LaTeX equivalence checking is internal.
FSRS scheduling ships library defaults; retention has never been studied inside the product.
